title: Rankings, ADP and Auction Prices: What to Trust in a 9-Cat League
brief: Why are Yahoo ranks, X-rank, ADP and straight 9-cat total rankings unreliable for our H2H 9-cat league, and how do points-league values leak into our draft room? It must show how to use rank versus market price to find value and when a gap between sites is an opportunity.
summary: No single list tells you what a player is worth in our 12-team H2H 9-cat auction. Yahoo X-rank, Yahoo ADP and straight 9-cat total rankings all mix in other formats or rest on flawed math. Use your own H2H category values to judge players, use Yahoo ranks and ADP only to predict what the room will do, and act only when the gap between the two is large.

sections.heading: Every number has a format behind it

paragraphs.text: A rank with no format attached tells you nothing. Player value changes between H2H categories, roto, Yahoo points, ESPN points and Sleeper. Labels like sleeper, bust or overrated only mean something once you know which format they come from. Before you use any list for our draft, ask one question: was it built for 12-team, 9-cat, head-to-head?

Yahoo shows two different ranks. X-rank is an expert list based on feel. It ignores your league format, and our draft room sorts by it by default. The separate 'rank' column comes from statistical projections and changes with league settings. Experts say X-rank sits somewhere between points value and category value without clearly being either. When you prepare, sort by the projection-based rank set to our settings, or better, by your own H2H 9-cat values. Never sort by X-rank.

Yahoo ranks and ADPs are the same for every format. They do not change with your league settings. Yahoo ranks some players with category leagues in mind and others with points leagues in mind. So you need to know both our settings and the logic behind the site's list.

sections.heading: Why straight 9-cat rankings fail in H2H

paragraphs.text: Several experts call ranking players by straight 9-cat totals the worst way to rank them. The results can be absurd. One such list had Giannis 69th or 70th per game, and nobody believes that. As one expert puts it: if you trust a 9-cat ranking, you have to accept every result it gives. If you would not take Giannis 69th, do not lean on that list to rank anyone else.

The main flaw is called 'nine-cat fluff'. The usual Z-score method, which counts turnovers, rates players who are strong in only a few categories too highly, and those players then get overdrafted. It can also go the other way. A low 9-cat rank can make a useful player look like a waiver-wire player, and the notes use Paolo Banchero as the example. Past finishes can mislead too. One expert called Turner's top-20 finish a flaw in the rankings and said Zubac's 9-cat rank did not show his real value.

Punt-based lists add a second trap. A one-category specialist can look like a top-100 player once you punt his weak categories. In a standard league that does not make him worth a roster spot. With 144 players drafted, do not pay for a specialist just because a punt list ranks him in the top 100.

The experts disagree on how much weight games played should get. One side says Yahoo's full-season total rankings overrate players who simply played a lot. Reed Sheppard, with 82 games, is their example of a player ranked far too high. The other side builds a head-to-head system around getting as many games as possible. That system cares less about low turnovers, says box-score values overrate blocks, steals and some percentages, and so ranks centers lower. Both sides agree that season totals are not H2H value. They differ on what should replace them. A rule that fits both: treat a high season-total rank built on volume alone with suspicion, and check how a player's value is spread across the categories.

Some experts go further than others. One never uses straight 9-cat rankings at all and says they are often quoted in bad faith. Others say only that the rankings can mislead and that they use other measures to judge value. If a player needs a 50-spot adjustment to reach his real value, the ranking system is the problem, not the player.

sections.heading: How points-league value leaks into our room

paragraphs.text: Yahoo ADP mixes points drafts and category drafts. Players who are valued for points leagues climb up category draft rooms and sit near the top of autodraft queues. Since Yahoo is the most-used platform, its ranks drive ADP. Rank and ADP also feed each other: when Yahoo drops a player's rank, his ADP tends to drift later too. Many drafters do not know why a player is ranked where he is, so bad ranks fool them.

The points-league profile is easy to spot. It is a high-usage, volume scorer with weak defensive stats and below-average efficiency. Such a player can be top 10 in points leagues but only a third-round value in category leagues. Usage tracks points-league value closely but category success much less. In our league, efficiency, assists, steals and blocks carry more weight. Do not spend early-auction money on a player whose value is mostly points. Price him at his category value and let someone else pay the points premium.

The leak also works in your favor. Some players are worth more in categories than in points. If the market blends both formats, their ADP leans toward their lower points value, and they come cheap in our room. Look for players with a big gap between their points value and their category value, especially when the site ranks or drafts them for the other format.

sections.heading: Rank versus market price: finding value

paragraphs.text: Keep two numbers apart. Your rankings and projections measure a player's quality. ADP is the market price and tells you when he will likely be available. One expert's example: if you rank a player 30th and his ADP is 70th, take him in the 50s, not at 30. Use Yahoo ranks and ADP as a forecast of what our room will do, not as a measure of value. How closely a league follows rank or ADP varies, and some leagues ignore both, so watch how our managers bid early on draft night.

Only act on big gaps. A gap of a few spots leaves no room for error. A gap of 15 to 20 spots protects you even if the player underperforms. In an auction, that means you stop bidding at the price of a slot between your rank and his market slot. Do not pay full price for your own rank when the room values him much lower.

ADP is an average, not a median. A player with an ADP of 50 goes after pick 50 in roughly half of drafts, and earlier in many others. An ADP of 46 means he goes outside the top 50 in some leagues. So do not assume a player will still be there at his ADP. If he is a core target, be ready to pay above his ADP slot.

Ours is an auction, so compare against auction data. Yahoo's auction price data currently differs a lot from its snake-draft ADP. Treat the two as separate markets and use the auction prices to set your bid limits.

Look for clusters. Players with similar category profiles, for example rebounds, blocks and FG%, should go around the same area. When the market spreads them far apart, the cheaper one is the value. If you miss the expensive one, the cheaper one gives you the same categories for less.

sections.heading: When a gap between sites is an opportunity

paragraphs.text: Rankings differ a lot between Yahoo, ESPN and Fantrax. Whether a player is a bust or a steal depends on the platform and format. Learn how each site presents its numbers and you can profit from the gaps.

Convert before you compare. ESPN's default leagues use 10 teams and 8 categories, so an ESPN rank is not a 12-team 9-cat rank. A gap is an opportunity only after you put both numbers on our format. If a player's ESPN ADP is far later than his rank, drafters are passing on him round after round. When you see the same pattern in our room, buy him.

Some gaps are just noise. A Yahoo ADP built on very few drafts can be inflated. Some Yahoo ADPs are skewed by dynasty leagues where the player is drafted in only a small share of leagues, so ignore those. ADPs also tend to repeat last season, so a gap built only on last year's results deserves a second look.

Timing for our draft on 2026-10-18: ADPs are not set by hand. They update every day from real drafts, and the ESPN numbers you see in your draft room are the current ones. Do not wait for a site to 'fix' an ADP you think is wrong. Re-check Yahoo auction prices and ADP in the last days before the draft, then lock in your bid limits.
